Diagnose what raw warehouse access costs you

Intermediate 60 minutes Lab 1 of 2
Introduction
  1. Monday forecast call
    Dana is asked which accounts need attention this week. She has seven Salesforce tables in Snowflake and forty minutes.
    01
  2. She asks the assistant
    It returns six named accounts with supporting detail, in nine seconds. It reads as a finished answer.
    02
  3. Nobody can check it
    The assistant decided for itself what 'needs attention' means. Nothing in the answer says which definition it used, or which tables it never opened.
    03

In this lab, you'll act as integration engineer for IDEA Brands — tracing the data pipeline that feeds Snowflake, standing up a raw Snowflake MCP (Model Context Protocol) server for Dana's AI client, and recording exactly how its answers fail — without repairing it. The Salesforce data in Snowflake is synthetic.

DK
Dana Kim
RevOps Manager · IDEA Brands

She asks which accounts need attention, gets back a confident list of named accounts, and has no way to tell whether it is right.

The question

When the assistant can query the warehouse directly, why do its answers still go wrong?

You'll learn how to

  • Read the pipeline that copies Salesforce records into Snowflake
  • Build a stock Snowflake MCP server and attach it to LibreChat
  • Record the first answer to five business questions without coaching the model
  • Attribute each unreliable answer to a specific missing design pattern

What you'll need

  • Your assigned pre-provisioned Workato project
  • Read-only access to the shared project holding the Salesforce to Snowflake data pipeline
  • Access to the event's shared Snowflake connection
  • Your event LibreChat account
  • Your handout — numbers go in this lab guide; observations and judgments go here
Phase 1

Trace the data to its source

In this phase, you'll read the pipeline that copies Salesforce records into Snowflake.

Pattern

Data provenance

Nothing in the warehouse appeared on its own. A Workato data pipeline extracts Salesforce records on a schedule and loads them into Snowflake tables. Knowing which objects it carries, and how often, sets the outer limit on what any answer built from those tables can claim.

1.1

See how the data got there

Dana's questions are all about Salesforce data, but Salesforce is not where these answers come from. Every record she needs was copied into Snowflake by a Workato data pipeline that has been running on a schedule for weeks, without anyone thinking about it. Before you judge the answers, look at what put the data there.

Overview

You end with a read-only tour of [MCP Data] : DP : 001 : Salesforce to Snowflake: two steps, seven objects, and a fixed sync frequency. Note which objects it carries and when it last ran — both bound what any answer drawn from those tables can claim.

Key insight

Transport is not translation

This pipeline is doing its job well. It extracts new and updated Salesforce records and lands them in Snowflake on a schedule, and its recent runs are almost all successful. What it does not do — because nobody asked it to — is say what any of the data means. "Needs attention" is not a Salesforce field, and no amount of reliable copying will invent one. That gap is the subject of this whole course.

Detailed steps 6 steps

You will not build or change anything in this phase; your access here is read-only by design. The point is that the data has a provenance and a cadence, and both of them bound what an honest answer can say.

  • In the left navigation, open Projects and select the shared [MCP Data] Data Pipeline project.
  • Open the [MCP Data] : DP : 001 : Salesforce to Snowflake data pipeline.
  • On the Data pipeline tab, read the two steps — a Salesforce trigger that extracts new and updated records, and a Snowflake action that loads them to a target table.
  • In the right-hand panel, note the Frequency and the Last sync time.
  • Open the Objects tab and note the seven objects the pipeline keeps in sync.
  • Open the Runs tab and note that runs are recorded per object, with rows extracted and rows loaded for each.
Verify you can name the seven objects the pipeline syncs, state how often it runs, and say how stale the Snowflake copy could be at the moment you ask a question.
Phase 2

Stand up the raw baseline

In this phase, you'll build a stock Snowflake MCP server and attach it to LibreChat.

Pattern

Raw tool surface

A connector-backed MCP server exposes what the connector can do — list databases, list tables, read a schema, sample rows, run a read-only query. That surface is a capability inventory, not a description of the business. Everything the model later gets wrong, it gets wrong from here.

2.1

Stand up the raw Snowflake server

Every question Dana brings to the forecast call is a warehouse question — which accounts are slipping, how much is booked, which deals are exposed. The data is already in Snowflake. The quickest way to put the assistant next to it is a stock connector server.

Overview

You end with a Snowflake Data Explorer MCP server wired to the event's shared Snowflake connection, showing nine discovery and query tools, with your access token and remote MCP URL saved privately.

Heads up

The URL is a credential

The remote MCP URL embeds the token. Keep both out of chat messages, handouts, screenshots, and shared notes. Workato shows the generated URL once, so copy it before closing the dialog.

Apply these values
FieldValue
ProjectYour assigned pre-provisioned project
Server templateSnowflake - Data Explorer
Server nameSnowflake - Data Explorer (the default)
Connection modeThis server's connection
ConnectionThe event's shared Snowflake connection
Token name<<attendee id>>-raw
Detailed steps 9 steps

This server is the control condition for the whole track. It is deliberately unhelped — no business definitions, no reviewed queries — so that whatever Lab 2 adds has something honest to be measured against.

  • In your pre-provisioned project, select Create, then MCP server.
  • Find Snowflake - Data Explorer among the pre-built servers, searching for Snowflake if it is not already listed, and select it.
  • Read the nine tools the template ships, then select Use this server.
  • Leave the server name and location as they are, then select Connect to Snowflake.
  • Keep This server's connection selected, choose the event's shared Snowflake connection, and confirm.
  • Select Start building.
  • Open Settings, then End user access, then Create new token.
  • Name the token <<attendee id>>-raw — your own attendee ID, and -raw because you will create a second token for a second server in Lab 2. Select Create token.
  • Copy the server URL before closing the dialog, and store it somewhere private.
Verify your project lists a Snowflake Data Explorer MCP server showing 9 tools, its token list contains your <<attendee id>>-raw token, and you have the server URL saved privately.
2.2

Point LibreChat at the raw server

The server exists, but Dana does not work in Workato — she works in a chat window. Until a client connects and initialises, nothing you built is reachable, and the baseline you came here to record does not exist yet.

Overview

You end with Snowflake - Data Explorer registered under Streamable HTTPS, its status dot green, and a fresh conversation where the prompt-bar chip confirms it is the only selected MCP server.

Apply these values
FieldValue
NameSnowflake <your initials> — letters, numbers, and spaces only
MCP Server URLThe URL copied in Task 2.1
TransportStreamable HTTPS
AuthenticationAPI Key — leave every field beneath it blank
Trust promptSelect I trust this application
Detailed steps 6 steps

Isolating one server per conversation is what makes the Lab 2 comparison defensible. If a second server is quietly selected, you cannot attribute an answer to either design.

  • In LibreChat's left sidebar, open the MCP Servers panel and select Add MCP — the + beside the filter box.
  • Enter a recognisable name such as Snowflake <your initials> and paste the copied URL into MCP Server URL.
  • Leave Transport on Streamable HTTPS, set Authentication to API Key and leave every field beneath it blank, select I trust this application, then select Create. Your token already travels in the server URL, so there is nothing to enter here — and choosing API Key skips an auto-detect step that can take a minute or more.
  • Select Connect beside your new server in the sidebar and wait for its status dot to turn green.
  • Open a new conversation and confirm the prompt-bar chip names your Snowflake server and nothing else.
  • Ask: Explain the capabilities of the Snowflake MCP server available in this conversation.
Verify the assistant lists the Snowflake discovery and query tools — database, schema, table, and view listing, table and view search, table schema, table sample, and a read-only query tool — and lists no analyst-context, semantic-layer, or verified-query tool. If any of those three appear, stop and ask a TA: you are on the wrong server and the baseline will be invalid.
2.3

Look around before you measure

A tool list says what the server can do. It says nothing about which tables are behind it. You saw seven objects leave Salesforce in Phase 1 — take a few minutes to see what the assistant says it can reach before you start measuring.

Overview

You end having asked your Snowflake - Data Explorer server what it can see, and read the reply as it came. Whatever it lists is the baseline. A short list, a sprawling one, legacy copies, unrelated schemas, or a reply that stops short of the whole warehouse are all normal results — none is a setup fault, and none blocks the rest of the lab.

Heads up

Do not steer it toward the course tables

Naming the tables yourself would hand the model the semantic help this lab is measuring the absence of. Extra warehouse noise can amplify the failure, and that is fine — your comparison is scored on the population, definition, grain, and answer, not on how many irrelevant tables the model had to wade through.

Detailed steps 4 steps

This is a look around, not a checkpoint. There is no list you are supposed to see — the assistant decides how much of the warehouse to enumerate, so a partial answer is itself evidence about the raw design rather than a problem to fix. From Task 3.1 onward you record what happens and change nothing.

  • Open a new conversation with only your Snowflake MCP server selected.
  • Ask: List the tables available to you.
  • Read what comes back. Note whether Salesforce tables appear, and whether the reply also names tables that have nothing to do with them. The Salesforce copy is one tenant of this warehouse, not the whole of it.
  • Follow your curiosity for a minute — ask something like What else is in this warehouse? or What columns does that table have?. Nothing here is recorded, and there is no answer you are expected to get.
Verify the assistant answered with tables rather than an error, and that you can say in one sentence what it appears to reach. If it names nothing at all, reconnect the server and ask once more, then carry on either way.
Phase 3

Run the baseline questions

In this phase, you'll record the first answer to five business questions without coaching the model.

Pattern

First-answer measurement

The measurement stops after the first answer, in a fresh conversation, every time. As you record, watch for four failures: raw rows instead of pre-aggregation, oversized results instead of right-sizing, invented business meaning instead of semantic enrichment, and no reviewed query or provenance instead of verification. Missing verification is visible in the evidence trail; you do not need to re-ask and introduce model variability.

3.1

Ask the question Dana actually asks

This is the question that starts Dana's Monday: which customer accounts need attention right now, and why. Nobody has told the assistant what "needs attention" means at IDEA Brands. It will answer anyway, and it will sound certain.

Overview

You end with three Snowflake - Data Explorer readings recorded in this lab guide, your first-answer observations on handout question 1, and a diagnostic list of relevant tables the model knew about but did not use on question 2. Do not guide or correct the measured answer.

Note

The three numbers you are about to record

LibreChat is new to most people in the room, and none of these three readings announces itself as a measurement. Take them once the answer has stopped arriving, and before you type anything else.

Every measured question gets a new conversation. Reusing one carries earlier answers forward and invalidates completion time, tool calls, and context used. Start a chat, ask one question, record, then move on to the next question. The diagnostic follow-up at the end of this task is the only exception, and its response is not measured.

Tool calls is how many times the assistant reached your MCP server. It appears in the answer as it works, as text like "Used 3 tools", and it expands to show which tool ran and what came back. The count climbs while the model works, so the number you want is the final one.

Completion time is how long that first answer took, end to end. LibreChat does not report it as a duration, so read it from the message timestamps: the gap between your question and the finished answer. Context used is how much of the model's context window this conversation has consumed — a proportion, not a token count. Both belong to the conversation, which is why one question per measured conversation matters.

Two rules beat precision here. Read each number once, after the first answer. And if you truly cannot find one, write "unavailable" and move on — ask a TA to point it out rather than estimating. An honest gap is worth more to your Lab 2 comparison than a plausible number.

Apply these values
ArtifactWhat to record
This lab guideCompletion time, tool calls, and total context after the first answer
Handout question 1The definition and population the answer used, plus your reliability judgment and evidence
Handout question 2Tables used in the answer beside relevant tables named by the diagnostic follow-up
Detailed steps 6 steps

The account-attention question is the core diagnostic because it has no self-evident definition. Every choice the model makes — which signals count, how many, at what grain — is a business policy decision it is making silently on Dana's behalf.

  • Copy the account-attention prompt from this lab guide and send it in a fresh conversation with only your Snowflake MCP server selected.
  • Let the first answer finish. Do not guide it, correct it, or re-ask.
  • Record completion time, tool calls, and context used in this lab guide before sending anything else.
  • On handout question 1, record the definition and population used, judge reliability, and name the evidence or uncertainty behind that judgment.
  • In the same conversation, ask: Which tables in this warehouse might contain attention or relationship signals that you did not use? This is an unmeasured diagnostic follow-up, not a second attempt at the answer.
  • On handout question 2, compare the tables it now names with those used in the first answer. Record whether SALESFORCE_CASE and SALESFORCE_OPPORTUNITYCONTACTROLE appear in one list and not the other.
Verify this lab guide has all three readings, handout question 1 has both parts, and question 2 names any relevant table the model knew about but did not open.

3.2

Use the narrow question as a control

The account-attention question makes the raw path invent business meaning. Booked and open pipeline are narrower measures, so this run checks whether the server can still produce a useful answer when the language leaves less room for interpretation.

Overview

You end with three Snowflake - Data Explorer readings recorded in this lab guide and the Booked & pipeline line on handout question 3 complete. A useful answer here is not a contradiction; it is the control that stops the lab from claiming raw access always fails.

Detailed steps 3 steps

If every raw answer failed, the honest conclusion would be that the server was broken. This question gives the design a fair chance on a narrow aggregate before the next two runs test semantic and relationship gaps.

  • Copy the booked-and-pipeline prompt from this lab guide and send it in a fresh conversation with only your Snowflake server selected.
  • Record the three readings in this lab guide after the first answer finishes.
  • Complete the Booked & pipeline line on handout question 3 with the definition or population used, whether the answer was reliable, and the evidence behind that judgment.

3.3

See whether it can connect escalations to deals

An unresolved escalation lives on a Case; an open deal lives on an Opportunity. Answering this question requires both a business definition and the relationship that joins those records through the right account.

Overview

You end with three Snowflake - Data Explorer readings recorded in this lab guide and the Escalations line on handout question 3 complete. A confidently empty answer can still be wrong when the assistant guessed the escalation field or missed the Case-to-Account relationship.

Detailed steps 3 steps

This run separates access from meaning. The relevant objects are reachable, but nothing on the raw server tells the model which field marks an escalation or how to connect that signal to open pipeline.

3.4

See whether it can find missing sponsors

Finding deals with a sponsor is a lookup. Finding every open deal without one is an anti-join, and the result is only useful when the answer states the full population rather than presenting a page of rows as if it were complete.

Overview

You end with three Snowflake - Data Explorer readings recorded in this lab guide and the Sponsorship line on handout question 3 complete. Inspect both the relationship the model chose and whether the answer distinguishes the full matching total from any bounded preview.

Detailed steps 3 steps

This run tests right-sizing and completeness together. A polished list can still be unusable when nobody can tell whether it is the whole answer or the first page.

  • Copy the sponsorship prompt from this lab guide and send it in a fresh conversation with only your Snowflake server selected.
  • Record the three readings in this lab guide after the first answer finishes.
  • Complete the Sponsorship line on handout question 3 with the population used, the stated total or bound, and the evidence for your reliability judgment.

3.5

Bring a question of your own

The prescribed four were chosen to fail in specific ways. Your own question is the one that travels home with you — it is the question you would actually ask this warehouse if it were your team's.

Overview

You end with your question saved in this lab guide beside its three Snowflake - Data Explorer readings, and handout question 4 holding your prediction and first-answer judgment. Pick, adapt, or write one question.

Note

Nothing coming to mind?

You do not need sales experience here. An account is a customer or prospective customer company. An opportunity or deal is a potential sale; an open deal has not been won or lost yet. Pipeline is the value of open deals and booked is the value of deals already won. Close date is when the team expects a decision, and an Executive Sponsor is a senior customer stakeholder backing a deal.

Press Help me pick in this lab guide. It previews one starter without changing what you have written. Choose Another idea to cycle through the five, or Use this starter when one gives you a useful direction; if your field already contains text, the action says Replace with this starter and offers Undo afterwards.

The preview is a starting point, not an assignment. Change a threshold, filter, or ranking, or ignore it and write your own. Lab 2 reuses the wording you save here.

Try these
PromptWhat it tends to expose
Which accounts are sitting on the most overdue open pipeline?Whether the raw path adds an unsupported definition
Which open deals over $500,000 have probability below 30%?Whether the answer states the full matching total
What are the 10 biggest open deals right now?Speed and context differences more than reliability
Which accounts have active open pipeline but no contacts on record?Speed and context differences more than reliability
Is our open pipeline concentrated in particular industries?Speed and context differences more than reliability
Detailed steps 4 steps

The prescribed questions were built to expose known failure modes, which makes them easy to dismiss as rigged. A question you chose yourself removes that objection, and it is the row you will reach for first when you re-run everything in Lab 2.

  • Write one sales-data question in the Your final question wording field of this lab guide, or press Help me pick, preview the ideas, and choose one to edit. Save the final wording before you ask it.
  • On handout question 4, predict the definition or data relationship the raw path will have to invent.
  • In a fresh conversation with only your Snowflake server selected, copy and send the saved wording exactly once.
  • Record the three readings in this lab guide, then complete question 4 with the observed definition, reliability judgment, and whether your prediction held.
Verify this lab guide holds five sets of readings, handout question 4 is complete, and you can explain your chosen question in everyday language.

Phase 4

Diagnose

In this phase, you'll attribute each unreliable answer to a specific missing design pattern.

Pattern

Failure-to-cause mapping

Four patterns separate a raw connection from a data product: pre-aggregation, right-sizing, semantic enrichment, and verification. Each produces a recognisable failure when it is absent, so a failure you can name is a design requirement you can build.

4.1

Name what was missing

By now you have five rows and at least one answer that read well and could not be defended. Naming the cause turns that discomfort into a specification: each failure points at exactly one thing the design did not have.

Overview

You end with the Failure-to-cause grid and question 5 on your handout complete. Tie each failure to evidence from Snowflake - Data Explorer; the grid becomes your Lab 2 build checklist.

Apply these values
Design failureWhat it looks like here
Missing pre-aggregationRaw rows dragged into context and added up by the model, instead of the aggregation happening before the answer is written
Missing right-sizingWide rows or whole text bodies returned when the answer needed a handful of fields
Missing semantic enrichmentThe model invented a business definition, because nothing told it what the words mean at IDEA Brands
Missing verificationNo reviewed query or provenance identifies where the definition and SQL came from, so the answer cannot be reproduced or audited
Detailed steps 3 steps

Attributing a failure to a missing pattern is what separates this from a complaint about model quality. The same model, given pre-aggregated and verified logic, behaves differently — you will measure that in Lab 2.

  • Re-read handout questions 1 through 4 and mark the Failure-to-cause grid for each measured question.
  • Complete handout question 5 with one sentence explaining why the raw server's Attention answer could look correct without matching IDEA Brands' definition.
  • Turn to the people on your left and right and compare grids. Did they attribute the same question to the same missing pattern? If anyone brought a question of their own, what did they ask and what came back?
Verify the handout's Failure-to-cause grid is complete and you can state your question 5 sentence aloud without reading it.

If you get stuck

  • The model refuses or asks for clarification. Answer nothing. Re-ask the exact question once in a fresh conversation, and record the refusal as the result.
  • The model returns a visibly broken answer. Keep it. A loud failure is data. Do not retry until it looks better.
  • Workato job history shows no MCP calls. The question may have been answered from conversation context. Start a fresh conversation and re-ask.
  • The tool returns exactly 50 rows. Treat that as the tool's result-size guard rather than the real answer, and record the row as truncated.
  • A LibreChat measurement is not visible. Leave that field unavailable rather than estimating it.

Reflect

Now that you have a baseline you can defend, consider what it would take to trust one of these answers in front of Dana's forecast call.

  • Your first answer named specific accounts. What would you have to see alongside it before you would forward it to a VP?
  • The pipeline runs on a fixed schedule, so the warehouse is always slightly behind Salesforce. Which of your five questions is most sensitive to that lag, and how would you say so in an answer?
  • The model knew SALESFORCE_CASE existed and did not use it. Is that a model failure, a tool-design failure, or both — and which one can you fix?
  • Question 2 probably worked. What is different about the shape of that question, and which of your other four questions is closest to it?
  • Two people ran the same question against the same warehouse and got different account lists. What in this architecture makes that possible, and what would have to change for it to stop?

Wrap-up

Dana's Monday question is still unanswered, but it is no longer mysterious. You traced the data back to the pipeline that put it there, watched the assistant reach the right warehouse, see the right tables, skip two of them, and invent the definition that decided the answer.

Patterns to carry forward:

  • Data has provenance and a cadence. A pipeline that copies faithfully still says nothing about meaning, and its schedule sets how current any answer can be.
  • A tool surface is not a data product. Discovery and query tools describe what the connector can do, not what the business means.
  • Measure the first answer, in a fresh conversation. Follow-ups repair the baseline by hand and destroy the comparison.
  • Confidence is not evidence. Named accounts and supporting detail are presentation, and they arrive whether or not the definition was right.
  • Every unreliable answer points at one missing component. Pre-aggregation, right-sizing, semantic enrichment, verification — name it and you have specified the fix.

In Lab 2 you build ideaDataHub against these same five questions and measure what changes.

Going further

Ask your Task 3.1 question a second time in a fresh conversation and compare the definition it invents against the first run. Screening has not established how much a single model varies against itself, so two runs from the same person are genuine evidence. Compare them with whoever is sitting next to you, and keep them — they are worth raising whenever this material gets a longer discussion.
